mastery.oneLine: A sustained joint glide applied by the therapist while the patient performs the movement that normally hurts, aiming for an instant pain-free result.
mastery.whatItIs: Mobilization With Movement (MWM) combines a gentle sustained glide with the patient's own active movement. You search for a glide direction that makes the previously painful movement easy and pain-free right now. If it works, you repeat it; if it does not, you stop.
mastery.analogy: It is like adjusting a sticky drawer while the person pulls it open. You try a small nudge in different directions until the drawer slides freely, instead of forcing it.
coreIdeas: The patient must be able to do the movement without pain while you apply the glide. No instant improvement means the glide is wrong; do not persist.
Hold the glide the whole time the patient moves, then repeat several times and finish with gentle overpressure only if painless.
The result should carry over: the movement stays better after you release (the 'long-lasting' rule).

terms.meaning: Pain-free, Instant result, Long-lasting. The three signs that an MWM is right.
A held, comfortable joint glide that does not oscillate.
A little extra gentle pressure at the end of movement, only if painless.
A checklist: Contraindications, Repetitions, Overpressure, Communication, Knowledge, Skill.

whenToUse: A clearly painful or restricted movement that is easy to repeat, for example painful gripping at the elbow or restricted ankle dorsiflexion.
Joints that can be glided safely in a direction that changes the movement at once.
whenNot: No immediate pain-free improvement after a few careful tries.
Unstable joints, fractures, infection or inflammation, and where glides are unsafe.
Any increase in pain, dizziness or neurological symptoms.

steps.title: Find the painful movement
steps.detail: Example: pain when gripping with the elbow extended in tennis elbow. Record the pain score.

steps.title: Search for the glide
steps.detail: Try a gentle glide (for example, sideways at the elbow) and ask the patient to repeat the movement.

steps.title: Check the PILL
steps.detail: The movement should become pain-free right now. If not, adjust the direction slightly, or abandon the technique.

steps.title: Hold and repeat
steps.detail: Hold the glide while the patient performs the movement 6-10 times.

steps.title: Add gentle overpressure only if painless
Release and retest
steps.detail: Check if the improvement stays. Teach a home version if suitable.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: about 6-10 repetitions, 2-3 sets, only if the movement is pain-free. Repeat for sessions if the benefit persists; if it fades quickly, rethink.

example.patient: Sana, 38, hairdresser, outer elbow pain when gripping her hairdryer.
example.assessment: Painful grip: 7/10. Pain-free grip is very weak.
example.treatment: You apply a gentle sideways glide of the forearm at the elbow while she grips. Pain falls to 1/10 during the grip. She repeats 10 times, 3 sets.
example.reassess: After release the grip is pain-free at 2/10 and stronger. You add strengthening exercises and review. Had the pain stayed at 7/10 you would have changed the glide or stopped.

mistakes: Continuing when pain does not drop instantly.
Applying the glide with so much force it hurts.
Giving no follow-up exercise so the improvement fades.

selfTest.q: No immediate improvement after several tries. What next?
selfTest.a: Change the direction slightly or abandon the technique.

mastery.recap: Glide, move, ask: if it is not pain-free and instant, it is not the right glide.
mastery.evidence: Small trials and reviews suggest short-term benefit for conditions such as tennis elbow and ankle stiffness, but the evidence quality varies. The mechanism is unclear and may include pain modulation.

depth.why: A sustained accessory glide is held while the patient actively performs the movement that was painful or restricted. The working hypothesis is a small positional fault or altered joint tracking corrected by the glide; an equally plausible explanation is combined mechanical and pain-modulating effects of the active movement under a glide. The result is tested on the spot, which makes it self-checking.
choose: Use when a specific active movement is painful or limited and can be changed immediately with a glide.
Follow the PILL response: Pain-free, Instant result, Long-lasting; if the result is not immediate, change the glide direction or stop.
Prefer Maitland when you cannot find a pain-free movement; prefer exercise alone when the problem is loading, not joint-related.
parameters: about 6-10 per set, up to 3 sets, with rest between sets
sustained, painless, direction chosen by trial (parallel or perpendicular to the joint plane)
added at the end of the pain-free range only if still pain-free
self-MWM with a belt or the patient's own hand when the glide is reproducible
depth.progress: Stop the glide as the movement stays pain-free; then add load and function. If pain returns, repeat the glide for a short block, never force.
measure: Pain during the target movement before, during and after the glide
Range of the movement that was limited, measured the same way each time
Durability: pain and range 24 hours later
depth.evidence: Trials show favourable short-term effects for several joints (for example lateral epicondylalgia, ankle sprain, cervical headache), but the positional fault explanation is unproven and quality of evidence is mixed. Treat it as a testable technique with a clear stop rule.
pitfalls: Persisting when pain is not abolished at once.
Using too much pressure that causes skin pain, which is not joint pain.
No active movement during the glide, which turns it into a different technique.
screen: Vascular signs in the neck and upper limb before any cervical technique

urdu.short: Mulligan Mobilization With Movement (MWM) mein therapist ek sustained accessory glide deta hai aur patient usi waqt apni active movement karta hai. Technique ka bunyadi test yeh hai ke movement ke dauran dard na ho ya wazeh taur par kam ho aur function mein faida nazar aaye. Agar sahi adjustment ke bawajood movement painful rahe, to technique ko zabardasti jari nahi rakhna chahiye.

details.heading: MWM ka basic idea
details.text: MWM passive accessory glide aur patient ki active movement ko combine karta hai. Therapist glide ki direction, angle ya assistance ko adjust karta hai; patient apni movement khud karta hai. Is liye yeh sirf therapist ke hand se joint move karna nahi, balkay movement ke response ko foran observe karna bhi hai.

details.heading: PILL principle
details.text: PILL ka matlab Pain-free, Immediate improvement, Long-lasting effect hai. Movement ideally pain-free honi chahiye, session ke andar improvement foran nazar aani chahiye, aur benefit glide hatane ke baad bhi kuch had tak retain hona chahiye. Agar yeh features na milen, to technique ki direction, suitability ya overall treatment plan par dobara ghour karein.

details.heading: Assessment se retest tak
details.text: Pehle patient ki ek relevant painful ya restricted movement ko baseline ke taur par note karein. Phir suitable accessory glide ke sath movement repeat karwayein. Force, direction aur position ko response ke mutabiq adjust karein. Overpressure sirf tab consider karein jab clinically munasib ho aur movement acceptable rahe. Aakhir mein glide ke baghair movement dobara check karein.

details.heading: Misal — sirf samjhane ke liye
details.text: Farz karein ek patient ko ankle dorsiflexion ke waqt discomfort aur restriction hai. Assessment ke baad therapist ek gentle glide ke sath patient se knee-forward movement karwata hai. Agar movement comfortable aur behtar ho, to therapist glide hatakar dobara test karta hai. Yeh fictional example hai, kisi specific ankle condition ke liye guaranteed result ya prescription nahi.

details.heading: Kab ehtiyat zaroori hai?
details.text: Acute highly irritable condition, postoperative restrictions ya uncertain joint stability mein pehle clinical screening aur relevant precautions zaroor dekhein. Fracture ya instability ka shak, serious neurological/vascular warning signs, ya aisa dard jo modification se acceptable na ho, mein technique jari na rakhein. Improvement ko exercise aur functional practice ke sath integrate karna aksar zaroori hota hai.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: Pehle woh active movement identify karein jo dard, stiffness ya function ki limitation ko reproduce karti hai. Mulligan Mobilization with Movement mein therapist accessory glide deta hai jab patient active movement karta hai. Glide ke saath movement comfortable honi chahiye; pain barhe to zabardasti continue na karein.

deeper.heading: Step-by-step concept
deeper.text: Comparable sign record karein, patient ko comfortable position dein, relevant joint par suitable glide apply karein aur patient se target movement karwayein. Direction aur contact joint aur movement ke mutabiq hotay hain; aik hi glide har patient par copy na karein. Belt ya self-mobilization ki exact placement supervised training mein seekhein.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur retest
deeper.text: Pain ke bawajood movement repeat karna ya sirf session mein behtar feel hone ko success samajhna aam ghalti hai. Range, pain aur relevant function ko pehle aur baad mein same tareeqe se compare karein. Agar behtari na ho to setup reassess karein; force bas barhana jawab nahi.

deeper.heading: Evidence aur expectations
deeper.text: Mulligan approach har musculoskeletal condition ka universal solution nahi. Response patient aur selected movement ke mutabiq vary kar sakta hai. Isay active rehabilitation aur broader management ke context mein dekhein, aur English chapter ki evidence limitations ko barqarar rakhein.

cue.wake: The patient's squat does not care how expensive your mobilization belt is.
cue.question: What should happen during a suitable MWM trial: more pain, or clearly easier movement?
cue.answer: Look for a comfortable, useful improvement while the patient moves; retest without help.
cue.easy: MWM = therapist's gentle guiding glide + patient's own active movement.
cue.remember: Guide and move. Remove the guide. Check again.

technique.storyHeadline: What if the painful movement could be tested differently—right now?

episode.patient: A footballer demonstrates the problem in one move: a squat that becomes uncomfortable around the knee. No lengthy mystery. The movement itself is your reference point, and the patient can tell you immediately whether it changes.
episode.decision: After screening, you trial a selected accessory glide while the patient actively repeats the squat. In the Mulligan approach, the response should be comfortable and meaningful. If it hurts, you modify or stop—never talk the patient into pretending it helped.
episode.retest: Repeat the squat without your glide. A smoother, more comfortable movement suggests a useful trial, which should be reinforced with active practice. If the effect vanishes, that is information too.
episode.spark: The squat is the final examiner, and it does not award marks for elegant hand placement.

aha.hook: Imagine a movement getting a second audition.
aha.analogy: The first squat hurts. Now repeat it with an appropriate accessory glide. If it becomes comfortable, the movement gets another chance—but the therapist still has to show the improvement lasts after the hands leave.
aha.challenge: The patient reports sharp pain during an MWM repetition. Should you finish the set anyway?
aha.reveal: No. A pain-free, beneficial response is central to the approach. Modify the glide or stop and reconsider.

weave.dialogue: Patient: 'So you hold my knee while I squat and it stops hurting?' Clinician: 'Maybe. But you get to be the judge, and the squat has to stay comfortable.' The patient looks pleased: finally, an examination they can grade themselves.
weave.watch: Watch the patient perform the identical task before and during the assisted glide. The clinician adjusts only within comfort. Then the contact disappears. The patient tries again alone. That unassisted repetition is where the story either delivers—or sends us back to the drawing board.
weave.method: The glide is not a secret joint-reset button. The intended Mulligan trial combines a carefully directed accessory movement with the patient's active action and an immediately favorable response. If pain climbs, abandon the hero pose.
weave.science: The patient's new experience could involve altered sensorimotor input, temporary symptom modulation or task confidence; a single successful squat cannot prove a joint was displaced and corrected.
weave.question: Assisted squatting is easier, but the pain returns immediately without the glide. Can you call the joint permanently corrected?
weave.answer: No. Treat it as a short-term trial response. Reassess dosage, independent movement and active rehabilitation, and avoid claims of permanent positional correction.
weave.closer: A skilled hand can open the door. The patient still has to walk through it.

patientPosition: Choose a position that reproduces the patient's meaningful painful movement safely: standing is often useful for weight-bearing problems; sitting or supine may be better when balance or irritability is an issue.
The patient must be able to actively perform the target movement while you maintain the accessory glide.
therapistPosition: Stand where you can maintain one consistent glide through the whole active movement.
Use a belt when it improves leverage and frees your hands, but make sure the belt does not compress sensitive structures.
handPlacement: Stabilize one segment and contact the other segment in the direction of the corrective accessory glide.
Your contact should be firm enough to maintain the glide but not so strong that it blocks active movement.
forceDirection: The direction is found clinically. Start with the most anatomically reasonable glide, then fine-tune angle and force until the active movement becomes clearly easier and preferably pain-free.
The glide remains sustained from the beginning to the end of the active movement.
applicationSteps: 1. Measure the painful or restricted active movement.
2. Apply a sustained accessory glide and ask the patient to repeat the movement.
3. If the movement is still painful, adjust the glide direction, angle, amount of force, stabilization or patient position.
4. When you find a pain-free/improved combination, keep the glide steady and repeat 6–10 slow repetitions.
5. Add gentle end-range overpressure only if the movement is already pain-free and clinically appropriate.
6. Remove the glide and immediately retest the original movement.
7. Teach a self-MWM only when the patient can reproduce the correct direction safely.
expectedResponse: Pain-free or clearly less painful movement during the technique and some carry-over after the glide is removed.
stopCriteria: Pain increases during the glide, symptoms peripheralize, the patient guards more, or there is no meaningful improvement after direction/angle correction.
commonMistakes: Accepting a painful MWM. The classic principle is pain-free application.
Changing the glide direction during the movement.
Using excessive force instead of searching for the correct angle.
Not checking whether the benefit remains when the manual glide is removed.
clinicalExample: Example: painful weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion. Apply a sustained posterior talar glide while the patient lunges forward. If the lunge becomes easier, repeat and then train squats, calf raises and balance.

mechanism.mechanismMap: Sustained accessory glide + pain-free active movement → altered joint sensory input + motor recalibration + reduced threat → immediate functional change
mechanism.simpleExplanation: MWM combines a manual glide with the patient's own movement. The most useful idea is not that the therapist permanently corrects a 'positional fault'. Instead, the glide changes sensory input and joint loading while the patient successfully performs a previously painful movement. That pain-free success can immediately change pain processing, motor output and confidence.
stepByStep: 1. A previously painful/restricted active movement is identified.
2. The therapist adds a sustained accessory glide.
3. The patient repeats the same movement while receiving altered joint and skin sensory input.
4. If the combination reduces pain, the nervous system receives a new 'safe movement' experience.
5. Motor output can change immediately: less guarding, smoother recruitment and greater range.
6. Repeated pain-free repetitions reinforce the new movement pattern.
7. If the benefit remains after the glide is removed, the intervention has produced useful short-term carry-over.
physiology: Changes in afferent input from joint, skin and muscle can alter spinal and supraspinal nociceptive processing.
Active movement adds motor-learning and sensorimotor components that passive mobilization does not provide.
Reduced pain during the task can reduce protective co-contraction and improve movement variability.
Context, expectation and the patient's experience of successful movement can contribute to the analgesic effect.
A pure 'positional fault correction' mechanism has not been established as the main explanation.
clinicalTranslation: The immediate response is the clinical test: if the movement is not better, the glide direction/technique should be reconsidered.
Repeated pain-free movement is more important than the therapist simply holding the glide.
Use the new movement window for strengthening or task practice.
myths: Do not tell the patient a bone was 'out' and is now 'back in'.
Do not accept painful repetitions because the technique is supposed to be pain-free/improving.
Do not assume the same glide direction works for every patient.
mechanism.evidenceNote: Immediate analgesic and movement effects are consistent with neurophysiological, sensorimotor and contextual mechanisms. The original positional-fault explanation remains a clinical hypothesis rather than a proven universal mechanism.

mechanismEvidence.summary: Manual therapy does not have one universal mechanism. Modern evidence supports interacting peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular, neuromuscular and contextual responses. The exact mechanism responsible for a patient's clinical improvement is often uncertain.
mechanismEvidence.sourceTitle: The mechanisms of manual therapy: A living review of systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews

room.arrival: The patient squats. Halfway down, their knee hurts. 'Exactly there.' You have your before-and-after test. The important movement is not hidden in a complicated machine.
room.touch: Trial an appropriate accessory glide as the patient repeats the action. Mulligan's intended response is comfortable and beneficial; adjust or stop if pain is reproduced.
room.retest: Remove your contact and invite the same squat. If the change is useful, build it into active exercise. If it lasts only under your hands, reconsider.
